questions.stem: Why is the solid added in excess during the method?

options.text: So that some undissolved solid remains, proving the solution is saturated
options.explanation: Solid left over after thorough stirring shows the water is holding all it can.

options.text: To make the solid dissolve faster
options.explanation: The amount added changes how much can dissolve, not how quickly it does.

options.text: To raise the temperature of the water
options.explanation: The water bath sets the temperature; the solid's job is saturation.

options.text: Because the balance needs a minimum mass to read
options.explanation: Excess serves the saturation guarantee, not the balance.

questions.stem: What error does pouring undissolved crystals into the evaporating basin cause?

options.text: The dissolved mass is overestimated, so the calculated solubility is too high
options.explanation: Crystals that never dissolved would be weighed as if they had, inflating the solute mass.

options.text: The solubility comes out too low
options.explanation: Extra solid adds mass, so the error pushes the value up, not down.

options.text: No effect, because the extra solid dissolves during evaporation
options.explanation: Evaporation removes water; it does not make the leftover solid part of the true dissolved mass.

options.text: No effect, because only dissolved matter is measured
options.explanation: Transferred crystals would sit in the basin and be weighed along with everything else.

questions.stem: What does heating to constant mass actually confirm?

options.text: That all the water has been evaporated from the basin
options.explanation: When two consecutive weighings agree, no water remains to be lost.

options.text: That the solid is completely pure
options.explanation: Constant mass speaks to water content, not to impurities in the solid.

options.text: That the balance is working correctly
options.explanation: The repeated readings test the sample's mass, not the instrument.

options.text: That the solution was truly saturated
options.explanation: Saturation was settled back at the stirring stage, long before evaporation.

questions.stem: Why must the saturated solution cool to exactly 30 °C before the portion is taken?

options.text: Because solubility depends on temperature, so the value only applies at the stated one
options.explanation: A solubility figure is only meaningful at the temperature it was measured at.

options.text: Because the evaporating basin could crack if poured hot
options.explanation: That is a safety courtesy, not the measurement reason.

options.text: Because solids stop dissolving above room temperature
options.explanation: Solids keep dissolving when warmed; in fact more goes into solution.

options.text: Because the balance reads incorrectly at other temperatures
options.explanation: The balance is not the constraint; the temperature-dependence of solubility is.

questions.stem: Why is the empty evaporating basin weighed before anything is added?

options.text: So every later reading can have the basin's own mass subtracted
options.explanation: Each combined weighing needs the empty-basin mass removed to reveal the contents.

options.text: To check the basin is clean and dry
options.explanation: Cleanliness matters, but the recorded mass exists for subtraction.
options.misconception: cleanliness check substituted for measurement purpose

options.text: To calibrate the balance against a known mass
options.explanation: Weighing the basin records its own mass; it calibrates nothing.

options.text: Because the method requires two identical basins
options.explanation: Only one basin appears in the method.

questions.stem: State what the leftover undissolved solid guarantees about the solution.
questions.modelAnswer: It is the guarantee that the solution is saturated.

questions.stem: State what may enter the pre-weighed evaporating basin.
questions.modelAnswer: Only clear solution — no undissolved solid.

questions.stem: Explain why this practical measures the solubility at one chosen temperature rather than across a range.
questions.modelAnswer: Because solubility changes with temperature — the practical measures a solid's solubility at one chosen temperature, so the solution must be held at that temperature for the measurement to mean one clean point.

questions.stem: A student weighs the dried basin once and records it immediately. State the flaw in that working, and the fix.
questions.modelAnswer: One weighing may still hold water — the basin must be reheated, cooled and reweighed until two masses agree (heated to constant mass), confirming all the water has gone.

questions.stem: With basin 25.00 g, basin plus solution 74.50 g and basin plus dry solid 37.00 g, what is the mass of water?

options.explanation: Solution 49.50 g minus solid 12.00 g leaves 37.50 g of water.
That is the whole solution; the dissolved solid must still come out of it.
options.misconception: solution mass mistaken for water mass

options.explanation: That is the solid's mass, not the water's.
Subtracting the empty basin a second time produces this meaningless figure.

questions.stem: In the same data, what is the mass of dissolved solid recovered?

options.explanation: Basin plus dry solid, 37.00 g, minus the empty basin, 25.00 g, gives 12.00 g.
That is the solution mass, solvent and solute together.
The empty basin's 25.00 g still has to be removed from that reading.
Adding the basin's mass instead of subtracting it doubles the error.

questions.stem: Why is the solid mass finally divided by the water mass and multiplied by 100?

options.text: To express the solubility in the standard unit of grams per 100 grams of water
options.explanation: The spec unit fixes the solvent at 100 grams, so the measured pair must be scaled to it.

options.text: To convert grams into centimetres
options.explanation: Mass and length are different quantities; no conversion links them here.

options.text: To work out the percentage of the solution that is solid
options.explanation: That separate calculation divides by the solution mass, not the water mass.

options.text: To cancel out the mass of the evaporating basin
options.explanation: The basin was already removed at the subtraction stage.

questions.stem: The calculation gives 24.2 percent. What does that number describe?

options.text: The solute's share of the whole solution by mass
options.explanation: Solute mass divided by solution mass, times 100, gives the solute's percentage of the solution.

options.text: The solubility in grams per 100 grams of water
options.explanation: That is the other result, 32.0; the percentage uses a different denominator.

options.text: The water's share of the solution
options.explanation: The water's share would be about 75.8 percent, the complement.

options.text: The increase in solubility per degree of warming
options.explanation: No gradient was measured; the figure comes from one set of masses.

questions.stem: What solubility do the recorded masses give for copper(II) sulfate at 30 °C?

options.text: 32.0 g per 100 g of water
options.explanation: Scaling 12.00 g of solid to 37.50 g of water gives 32.0 g per 100 g of water.

options.text: 24.2 g per 100 g of water
options.explanation: That is the percentage figure misread as a solubility.

options.text: 49.5 g per 100 g of water
options.explanation: The solution mass was scaled, not the solid mass.

options.text: 12.0 g per 100 g of water
options.explanation: That quotes the raw solid mass without the scaling to 100 grams of water.

questions.stem: State how the mass of the solution is obtained from the weighings.
questions.modelAnswer: Mass of solution is the filled basin minus the empty basin.

questions.stem: State how the solubility figure is calculated from the solid and water masses.
questions.modelAnswer: The solid mass is scaled up to 100 grams of water (solid mass divided by water mass, then multiplied by 100).

questions.stem: Explain why the solid mass is scaled to exactly 100 grams of water.
questions.modelAnswer: Because solubility values are stated in grams per 100 grams of solvent (water), so scaling to 100 g makes the number comparable with tables and curves.

questions.stem: A basin weighs 30.00 g empty, 55.00 g with solution, and 41.00 g with dry solid. State the mass of water in the sample.
